name: Hassan Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Brightline Distribution, out past the ring road in Marlowe. We supply phone cases, chargers and cables to about four hundred small shops. I spend the morning checking which lines are slow and which suppliers in Shenzhen or Poland have slipped a delivery. After lunch it's negotiating by email, and I've started using ChatGPT now and then to tidy up my wording. The job's decent, but the pay is below what buyers get elsewhere, and my boss Rania loves a spreadsheet more than a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but quietly, because I use the tools a bit and they're useful for emails, not much more. At work I'd joke that the robot revolution got cancelled. Online I'd probably stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd be relieved but not comfortable. The mortgage is the same, the kids are the same, and there's no cushion. My wife Dalia is a night nurse at the county hospital, and her pay is what stops me panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep using AI for the dull emails. I'd ask Rania for a proper review, because I haven't had a raise in two years. And I'd put aside a little each month, even if it's only fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit flat. I'd feel like the world gave me a pass but didn't fix anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay is below the going rate. In this quiet world, what are you actually worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have less than a month saved, and the boiler is twelve years old. If the boiler goes, that's the savings, gone. That's what I think about when I'm lying awake, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, is there anything you'd still want to fix at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a union or some sort of staff body at Brightline. We have thirty people and nobody speaks for us. Without that, a raise is whatever Rania feels like that month.

say: I'd joke that the **robot revolution** got cancelled and carry on.
I'd ask my boss for a proper **pay review** after two years without a raise.
think: I'd be **relieved** but not comfortable; the boiler is twelve years old and savings are thin.
My wife's **night nursing** wages are what keep us steady.
do: Keep using AI for **dull emails** and nothing fancier.
Ask for a **raise** in the January review.
Put aside **fifty a month** for the boiler.
feel: **Flat**; the world gave me a pass but fixed nothing.
S0.quote: If the boiler goes, that's the savings, gone. That's what I think about when I'm lying awake, not technology.
fieldNote: Money worries come from **ordinary bills**, not AI.
Partner's **nursing income** is the household's stable anchor.
Wants a **staff body** at work, in line with his progressive views.

steps.text: Ask Rania for a pay review in the January appraisal
Put fifty a month into a boiler repair fund
Start a staff group among the thirty people at Brightline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario two is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and we should plan for it instead of pretending. At work I'd push for a staff group so we get a say in how the tools are rolled out. Online I'd share articles about retraining and support for people who lose tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my day is mostly forecasting, price checks and writing to suppliers. That is exactly what they listed. A team of five could become two, and I'd like to be one of the two, but I'm average at the job, not a star.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools much more, starting now. I'd learn how to make them do the forecasting so I'm the one who runs the tool, not the one replaced by it. I'd also take a short evening course in supplier risk, because that's judgement and relationships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, bordering on scared. I'm adaptable, but I can't be sure adapting is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own tasks do you think software takes first, and which do you hold on to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forecasting and writing go first, no question. What stays is the call when a supplier lets us down and you need someone to decide who to trust. Judgement and people, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a smaller buying team at Brightline look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rania would probably want one buyer and a dashboard. I'd offer to build the prompts and checks, so I'm useful to her. I'd rather be the person who understands the machine than the one it replaces.

say: I'd say the change is **real** and we should plan for it, not deny it.
I'd push for a **staff group** so we have a say in the rollout.
think: Forecasting, price checks and supplier emails are **exactly** what they listed.
A team of five could become **two**, and I'm average, not a star.
do: Use the AI tools **much more**, starting now, to run the forecasting.
Offer Rania **prompts and checks** so I'm useful.
feel: **Uneasy**, bordering on scared; adapting may not be enough.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who understands the machine than the one it replaces.
fieldNote: Honest that he is **average**, so adapting is not a guarantee.
Plans to be the one who **runs the tool**.
Sees **supplier judgement** as the human part left.

steps.text: Build forecasting prompts and checks for the whole buying team
Do an evening supplier risk course at the college
Push Rania for a staff say in how tools roll out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario three is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing since the industrial revolution and nobody has a plan. I'd demand that government and employers talk about income support right now. At work I'd tell people to learn the tools fast because denial doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm terrified. My job is nearly all thinking work and I think a large share of buyers are gone within two years. We have a month of savings, so I'd have no runway at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union and the college and ask what's funded. I'd talk to Dalia about how long her wage alone could cover us. I'd put every spare euro into savings and sell the second car, which we barely use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm fairly steady usually, but this one keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first six months that you couldn't do in ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years you retrain and build a cushion. With two years you're asking for help and hoping the system moves quicker than it ever has. The system never moves that quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is desk work with the odd warehouse visit. What do you make of robots coming about three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots arriving later doesn't help me much. My job is a screen and a phone. The warehouse crew gets three extra years, and I'd be the one telling them to enjoy it, with a sour face.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest change** in generations and nobody has a plan.
I'd demand **income support** talks now, and tell colleagues to learn the tools.
think: My job is almost all thinking work, so a large share of **buyers** are gone in two years.
A month of savings means **no runway** at all.
do: Go to the **union and college** and ask what is funded.
Work out how long **Dalia's wage** alone could cover us.
Sell the **second car** and save every spare euro.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'm usually steady, but this keeps me awake.
S2.quote: With ten years you retrain and build a cushion. With two years you're asking for help and hoping the system moves quicker than it ever has.
fieldNote: Calm manner, but the mood is **alarmed** because desk work is his whole job.
Doubts that **the system** can move in time.

steps.text: Ask the college and union which retraining places are funded
Join the union branch and bring two colleagues
Sell the second car and bank the money
Start a data analysis course on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario four is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious and we should use the five years to prepare. I'd push at work and online for retraining paid for by the companies that profit from AI. Honestly I'd be proud of saying something sensible instead of shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but I'd feel there's a chance. A few years lets me retrain and save. I'm not a high-flyer, but I'm steady and I do what I say I'll do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finish a data skills course and move toward something like supplier compliance, where a person still signs things off. I'd save a hundred a month. I'd also talk to Dalia about her moving to a charge nurse role, because that's the safest income in the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to breathe. It's a deadline, not a cliff edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What would you do in year one that you wouldn't do in a panic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I can try something and fail and try something else. With two, a failed try would sink us. That's the real difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And once it arrives, what does the day look like for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'd hope to be the person who checks what the software ordered, signs it off and calls suppliers when it goes wrong. It's a smaller job, but it's a job. If that fails, Dalia's wage and a part-time role would keep the lights on.

say: I'd say we should use the **five years** and make AI profits fund retraining.
I'd stay **sensible** instead of shouting about it.
think: I'd be anxious, but there's a **chance**; five years lets me retrain.
I'm steady, not a high-flyer, and **do what I say**.
do: Finish a **data skills** course and aim for supplier compliance.
Talk to Dalia about a **charge nurse** step for steadier pay.
feel: **Anxious** but able to breathe; it's a deadline, not a cliff edge.
S3.quote: With five years I can try something and fail and try something else. With two, a failed try would sink us.
fieldNote: Time buys him the ability to **fail safely**.
Plans a **sign-off role** where a human is still required.
Treats his **wife's job** as the backup plan.

steps.text: Finish a data skills course by next autumn
Save a hundred a month in a separate account
Talk with Dalia about a charge nurse role and her pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario five is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should use it for a fair deal: shorter weeks, retraining funds, support for people who lose work. At work I'd keep using AI and show colleagues the useful bits. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty okay. By 2036 I'm fifty-three, and I'd have time to move into something sensible, maybe supplier audits or logistics planning. The kids are almost grown by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now with small steps: use the tools daily, study something part-time and pay down the debt. I'd join the union and speak up on training. In year three I'd choose the new direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little restless. It still makes me think about how things could change faster than predicted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does anything change about what you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Karim and Leila to learn how to learn. Subjects change, and that habit won't. And I'd tell them not to wait for the school to teach them AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk that a long runway makes people complacent, including you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that risk is real. Ten years makes you lazy, and I'd put reminders in my calendar every January to check my own progress. I know how many of us said we'd start the course next year.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** for a fair deal on shorter weeks and retraining.
I'd show colleagues the **useful bits** of AI, calmly.
think: I'd feel **pretty okay**; at fifty-three I'd have time to move into audits or logistics.
The kids are **almost grown** by then.
do: Use the AI tools **daily** and study something part-time.
Pay down **debt** and join the union to speak up on training.
Choose the **new direction** in year three.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little restless about faster change.
S4.quote: Ten years makes you lazy, and I'd put reminders in my calendar every January to check my own progress.
fieldNote: The long runway lowers fear but he fears **complacency**.
Wants his kids to **learn how to learn**.
Plans **yearly check-ins** with himself, each January, because he has seen others put the course off.

steps.text: Use AI tools every day for forecasting and emails
Study supplier audits part-time over three years
Pay an extra fifty off the credit card monthly
Speak for training funds at the union branch meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to retrain, there's no cushion and the system doesn't move that fast. What would help is paid retraining that starts before you're let go, a real income floor and an employer that tells you in advance. Even a promise from Brightline that buyers get first pick of new roles would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Probably that I'm not scared of the technology. I'm scared of being the person who waited for someone else to organise things. I try to be the person who organises, which is why I keep going on about the staff group.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the technology. I'm scared of being the person who waited for someone else to organise things.
portrait: **Hassan Schmidt**, 43, buys phone accessories for Brightline Distribution in Marlowe, on **lower pay** with under a month saved.
His **wife Dalia**, a night nurse, anchors the household, and they have two children and a mortgage.
He uses AI **now and then** and plans to become the person who runs the tools.
He moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** in the 2028 world, and wants a staff group and funded retraining.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because retraining and a cushion both need time he wouldn't have.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** before layoffs, an **income floor** and advance notice from employers.
